strengths: Addresses an underexplored and important problem: how LLM-powered embodied agents use episodic memory for personalized assistance, beyond conventional instruction-following.
Introduces MEMENTO, a two-stage memory evaluation framework (memory acquisition vs. memory utilization) that helps isolate the effect of memory use on task performance.
Categorizes personalized knowledge into object semantics and user patterns, enabling fine-grained analysis of different memory-reasoning challenges.
Conducts experiments across six frontier and open-source LLMs, with additional analyses on top-k retrieval, memory quality, ambiguous instructions, and qualitative success/error cases.
Provides useful empirical findings and detailed prompts/implementation setup, offering practical insights for future personalized embodied agents.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the framework is built heavily on existing benchmarks (PartNR) and simulators (Habitat 3.0); the two-stage evaluation design is intuitive but incremental rather than a fundamental technical advance.

Dataset scale is modest: 12 scenes, 201 unique acquisition/single-memory episodes, and only 36 joint-memory episodes; this raises concerns about statistical robustness and the strength of conclusions drawn from small joint-memory subsets.

Potential bias from GPT-4o-based data generation and filtering: instructions/personalized knowledge are generated by GPT-4o, and episodes where GPT-4o fails repeatedly are filtered, which may favor GPT-4o-style behavior and exclude difficult or ambiguous cases, compromising fairness and the claim of comprehensive evaluation.

Evaluation scope is narrow: it uses high-level planners with oracle skills and no visual perception or low-level control, so it does not assess full embodied agents under realistic perception/action uncertainty.

Lacks comparisons to dedicated memory-augmented agent methods (e.g., MemGPT-style, A-Mem, or other episodic memory frameworks), making it unclear whether observed failures are due to LLMs in general or to the absence of specialized memory architectures.

The retrieval setup forcibly includes the correct memory in the top-5, so it does not evaluate retrieval accuracy; the top-k analysis mainly tests robustness to distractors rather than memory retrieval capabilities.
Main results lack statistical significance tests or confidence intervals, especially for joint-memory tasks where sample sizes are small, so reported performance drops may be noisy.
Reproducibility is limited: it is unclear whether the MEMENTO dataset and code will be publicly released, and API-based generation of instructions and memories may be difficult to reproduce exactly.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: memory utilization for personalized embodied agents.
The two-stage acquisition/utilization design is a reasonable conceptual attempt to isolate instruction interpretation with and without prior personalized knowledge.
Categorizes personalized knowledge into object semantics and user patterns, with subcategories, providing useful axes for analysis.
Builds a sizeable (438 episodes) evaluation set on Habitat 3.0/PartNR with distractor objects and joint-memory tasks.
Evaluates multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs, reports standard metrics, and includes analyses (top-k, knowledge type, case studies, memory quality, trajectory, ambiguity).
Appendix provides implementation details, prompts, and limitations/societal impact discussion.
weaknesses: The memory acquisition stage simply injects personalized knowledge into the instruction, so the agent never has to induce personal semantics from observed behavior. The benchmark thus tests retrieval/application of an explicit prior sentence more than episodic memory or personalization, weakening the central framing.

Dataset quality control filters out episodes where GPT-4o fails five consecutive attempts (31 episodes, 13.4%), which biases the benchmark toward GPT-4o's capabilities and inflates acquisition-stage performance; a benchmark should not be constructed by filtering on a target model's failures.

The retrieval setup guarantees inclusion of the correct memory by randomly replacing a retrieved memory if needed, so main results do not evaluate retrieval and instead assume oracle retrieval. This limits realism and makes top-k claims narrower than presented.
Evaluation is statistically weak: joint-memory tasks have only 36 episodes; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for main results, and some model differences may be noise.

Several claims are overstated or unsupported by the results: e.g., the text says all models show >20% success-rate drops, but GPT-4o single-memory drops only 9.9%; the validation without retrieval only shows utilization instructions are underspecified, not that MEMENTO measures memory utilization.

Limited comparisons and baselines: no alternative memory systems/retrieval methods or personalized-agent baselines beyond the same LLM planner with different LLMs; ablations are mostly post hoc and small-scale.
Reproducibility is incomplete: no clear release statement for dataset/code; dataset generation relies heavily on GPT-4o and manual/model-based filtering, making exact reproduction difficult.
Presentation has multiple clarity issues (MEMENTO/Memento inconsistency, typos such as 'declaration stage', 'action action trajectories', unclear figure/table references, appendix formatting).

Significance for real-world personalization is reduced by acknowledged simplifications: simulator only, no visual perception, oracle low-level skills, and explicit personalized knowledge rather than learning from user interaction.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely evaluation framework (MEMENTO) for personalized embodied agents, focusing on episodic memory utilization for personalized assistance.
Provides a systematic two-stage evaluation design (Memory Acquisition vs. Memory Utilization) that isolates memory utilization from instruction-following and enables quantification of memory impact.
Comprehensively categorizes personalized knowledge into object semantics (ownership, preference, history, groups) and user patterns (routine, preference), enabling fine-grained analysis.
Constructs a benchmark dataset with careful scene augmentation, distractor objects, and quality control, spanning 12 scenes and 438 episodes.

Conducts extensive experiments across six LLMs (proprietary and open-source), using multiple metrics (PC, SR, Planning Cycles, Sim Steps) and thorough analyses, including knowledge-type, top-k, memory-quality, trajectory, and ambiguous-instruction studies.
Reports clear and important findings: even GPT-4o suffers a 30.5% success-rate drop in joint-memory tasks, user-pattern tasks are particularly challenging, and irrelevant memories act as distractors.
Provides implementation details, prompts, skill library descriptions, evaluation protocol, and license information, supporting reproducibility.
Acknowledges limitations and societal impacts, including privacy concerns around episodic memory in personalized agents.
weaknesses: Dataset size is modest (201 acquisition, 201 single-memory, 36 joint-memory episodes) and was generated/filtered using GPT-4o, potentially biasing toward GPT-4o capabilities and reducing benchmark difficulty and discriminative headroom.

The memory retrieval setup forces inclusion of the correct memory by randomly replacing one retrieved memory if the correct one is not initially retrieved, so retrieval accuracy is not evaluated; this limits claims about full memory utilization in realistic deployment.
The evaluation uses oracle low-level skills and deliberately excludes visual perception, assessing only high-level planning and memory reasoning rather than full embodied task execution.

No comparison to alternative memory mechanisms or retrieval methods; baselines are variations of LLM models under the same memory architecture, so the benchmark does not evaluate different memory designs.
Reproducibility is somewhat limited by the absence of an explicit public dataset/code release statement, despite detailed prompts and implementation information.

User-pattern tasks depend on trajectories that contain the answer from the acquisition stage, and the memory-quality analysis shows sensitivity to noisy retrieved memory, which may inflate the role of trajectory details and complicate interpretation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: personalized assistance in embodied agents through memory utilization, with a clear two-stage evaluation framework (MEMENTO) that isolates memory effects by sharing scene and goal while varying instruction specificity.

Provides a substantial empirical study across six LLM-powered agents, multiple task types (single-memory, joint-memory), and analyses of key bottlenecks such as information overload from increased top-k retrieval and coordination failures in joint-memory tasks.
Introduces a reasonably well-designed benchmark built on Habitat 3.0 and PartNR, with distractor objects and quality-control procedures, plus a human baseline to validate task solvability.

The proposed hierarchical knowledge-graph user-profile memory shows promising improvements across models and task types, and the paper explicitly separates object-semantics and user-pattern knowledge, which is a useful conceptual distinction.
Reproducibility is supported by code release, detailed appendices, prompts, and dataset-generation documentation; limitations and societal impacts are discussed.
weaknesses: Ethical/IRB concern: the main Ethics Statement says the work involves no human subjects, but Appendix E.1 describes recruiting four undergraduate participants for a human baseline. Consent, IRB approval, and participant-data handling are not documented, which is a serious unresolved issue for a top-tier venue.

The proposed user-profile memory is not sufficiently ablated or compared against strong alternative memory architectures. It is unclear whether gains come from the hierarchical knowledge graph, cleaner extracted personalized knowledge, or simply additional LLM-based preprocessing; no component-level ablation or graph-accuracy evaluation is provided.

The main evaluation guarantees that gold memories are included in the top-k retrieval set, which simplifies the memory-utilization problem and may overestimate practical performance. Realistic retrieval is only partially explored in the appendix.

Dataset construction filters out episodes where GPT-4o fails repeatedly, potentially biasing the benchmark toward GPT-4o-friendly tasks and removing hard but legitimate cases. Quality-control reliability is only moderate on average (Krippendorff's alpha 0.69, with triviality and redundancy below 0.6).

The memory-design experiments use small samples (e.g., 30 episodes for format simplification, 36 joint-memory tasks), and the paper reports improvements without statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or error bars, making 'substantial improvements' claims harder to assess.

The approach relies heavily on oracle perception and motor skills and language-only observations, which limits claims about real embodied agents. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the gap between the evaluation setting and practical deployment remains large.

The proposed knowledge-graph memory is largely described in the appendix, and its construction depends on LLMs for extraction, update decisions, and reformulation; failure modes of this pipeline and sensitivity to LLM quality are not systematically evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem: personalized assistance in LLM-powered embodied agents, with memory utilization as a key capability.
Proposes MEMENTO, a two-stage evaluation framework that shares scene/goal and varies instruction specificity to isolate memory utilization.
Evaluates multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs across two dimensions, object semantics and user patterns, and reports consistent limitations.
Identifies practical bottlenecks such as information overload under larger top-k retrieval and coordination failures in joint-memory tasks.
Provides extensive appendix material, including implementation details, prompts, dataset construction, and a code link, supporting reproducibility.
Includes ethics and reproducibility statements, showing awareness of privacy and deployment concerns.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the benchmark is built by modifying PartNR with GPT-4o-generated personalized knowledge, and the proposed hierarchical knowledge-graph user-profile memory is a relatively straightforward structured memory design rather than a fundamentally new method.

Small evaluation scale: 438 total episodes, only 36 joint-memory tasks, and memory-design experiments using only 30 sampled episodes are insufficient to support strong empirical claims or model rankings.

Weak baselines and ablations for the proposed memory module: there is no comparison to existing memory/retrieval systems such as MemGPT, A-Mem, RAG-style memory, or other structured memory architectures, and no ablation isolating the KG structure from additional context/retrieval effects.

Confounded experimental design: joint-memory tasks combine multiple memories with longer and more complex instructions, so 'coordination failures' are not cleanly isolated; similarly, the summarization experiment conflates loss of trajectory-level in-context learning with memory extraction quality.

Overstated claims: the 'substantial improvements' from user-profile memory are presented mainly as a figure with no numerical table, effect sizes, or significance tests, making it difficult to judge practical impact.

Realism and validity concerns: use of oracle perception/motor skills and guaranteed inclusion of gold memories in top-k limits claims about real embodied agents; real retrieval noise is only explored in appendices and not integrated into main conclusions.

Dataset quality concerns: personalized knowledge is LLM-generated and filtered with only moderate inter-rater reliability (average Krippendorff's alpha 0.69, with some criteria at 0.57); the human baseline is very small (four participants, 20 tasks).

Proposed memory module details are largely relegated to the appendix, and its update/retrieval algorithms are not rigorously validated in the main paper; failure modes, scalability, and robustness are underexplored.
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the main comparisons; many reported differences may be within noise given the small sample sizes.
Reference and formatting issues reduce clarity (e.g., inconsistent citations and corrupted-looking references), suggesting insufficient care in manuscript preparation.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem: memory utilization for personalized embodied agents, and frames it through two clear dimensions (object semantics and user patterns).

The MEMENTO evaluation framework is well motivated, with a two-stage acquisition/utilization design that attempts to isolate memory-use capabilities rather than confounding them with low-level perception or motor failures.

The empirical analysis is broad and useful: six LLMs of different scales are evaluated, and the paper provides informative findings on object semantics vs. user patterns, information overload under larger top-k, and joint-memory coordination failures.
The proposed hierarchical knowledge-graph-based user-profile memory is a plausible architectural direction, and the reported improvements across models and task types are encouraging.
The paper includes a substantial appendix, human baseline, robustness checks, retrieval-strategy analysis, and reproducibility/code details, which strengthens the overall empirical contribution.
The writing is clear and the paper is well organized, with an appropriate discussion of limitations and ethical/privacy considerations.
weaknesses: The central memory-architecture contribution is relatively lightly evaluated: the user-profile memory results are mostly summarized in a figure, with limited ablation of the graph structure, retrieval design, or separate contribution of episodic vs. profile memory.

The main evaluation uses synthetic personalized knowledge generated by GPT-4o, with moderate inter-rater reliability (average Krippendorff's alpha 0.69). This raises questions about whether the findings generalize to naturally occurring user personalization.

The main benchmark experiments guarantee gold memory retrieval by replacing retrieved candidates, which isolates memory utilization but may overestimate real-world performance where retrieval itself is a bottleneck.

The agent uses oracle perception and motor skills, so the study deliberately ignores substantial sources of real embodied failure. This is acknowledged but limits direct applicability to real embodied agents.

There is little comparison to existing memory architectures for LLM agents (e.g., MemGPT, A-MEM, MemoryBank, or other episodic-memory/RAG baselines), making it harder to judge whether the proposed memory module is genuinely superior to alternative designs.

The memory-design experiments appear to use a relatively small sampled subset (e.g., 30 episodes in the simplification study), and statistical significance/error bars for the proposed user-profile memory improvements are not clearly reported.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: for example, the paper attributes improvements to 'separately managing personalized knowledge,' but does not fully disentangle whether gains come from structured knowledge, better retrieval, extra context, or the LLM used in memory construction/retrieval.
